messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 19
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Environmental Scientist
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
- Pcl5: 36

He is a 19-year-old Middle Eastern man who comes across as composed at first, with a careful way of speaking and a habit of weighing each answer before he gives it. Over several sessions, it becomes clear that this restraint has long been part of how he survives. He is married now, and he works as an environmental scientist, spending much of his day in the field collecting samples, noting changes in soil and water, and trying to understand systems that are damaged but still functioning. He says he likes the work because nature does not yell, does not lie, and does not suddenly turn angry without warning. He can trust patterns in the landscape in a way he never could trust the adults who raised him.

He grew up in a home where physical punishment was not occasional but routine, delivered by a caregiver who believed force was discipline and humiliation was character-building. As a child, he learns to read footsteps in the hallway, tone of voice, and the set of a jaw. A door closing too hard can mean trouble. A missed instruction, a broken object, or simply being in the wrong place at the wrong time can bring shouting, grabbing, slapping, or worse. He remembers staying small on purpose, making himself quiet and invisible, trying to anticipate every mood shift. Even then, he often cannot prevent the violence. He describes living with the sense that his body is always bracing for impact, even when he is sitting still.

As he gets older, he becomes skilled at leaving himself mentally. He stares at walls, counts patterns in the ceiling, and focuses on details around him so he can feel slightly less present when the abuse starts. He stops crying because crying seems to make things worse. He also stops asking for help, partly because help never comes and partly because he cannot imagine anyone believing how bad it is. He learns early that reporting what happens at home carries its own risk, so he keeps the fear inside and develops a private rule: endure, do not react, do not give anyone another reason.

Now, years later, he still carries that rule into adult life. He wakes easily, especially to sudden sounds. In the night he sometimes sits up before he is fully awake, heart pounding, not immediately sure where he is. His wife has learned to speak to him softly when she approaches unexpectedly, because if she comes up behind him without warning he flinches hard, then looks embarrassed afterward. He apologizes quickly, even when no apology is needed, as though he has been caught doing something wrong. He says he is always aware of exits in a room, always aware of who is standing too close, and he dislikes having his back to people. Crowded places leave him tense and irritable. In stores or on public transit, he scans faces and hands before he can settle enough to think about what he needs.

At work, he is highly competent and praised for being observant, but his vigilance has a cost. If a supervisor raises a voice, even in frustration at something unrelated to him, his chest tightens and his mind empties. He can continue working, but afterward he has trouble concentrating and feels as if he has returned to a younger version of himself who is waiting to be hurt. He keeps his expression controlled, yet internally he is often angry in ways that surprise him. Sometimes the anger arrives after a small trigger, such as a slammed car door or a sudden command, and he is left feeling ashamed of the intensity of it. Other times he feels numb, especially when conversations turn toward family. He gives short answers about his childhood and changes the subject, not because he does not remember, but because remembering brings a pressure in his throat and a heaviness behind his eyes.

He married young, and his relationship is one of the few places where he allows himself to be seen. Even there, trust is not easy. He wants closeness but fears it at the same time, and he can become distant when he feels overwhelmed. His wife notices when he withdraws into silence after a bad dream or after speaking with someone from his past. He says the memories do not come like orderly stories; they arrive in fragments, sensations, and body reactions, as if his nervous system remembers before his mind does. On difficult days he avoids calls, avoids family gatherings, and sometimes works late so he does not have to return immediately to a house where the quiet can feel too exposed.

What stands out most is how much effort he expends to appear unaffected. He functions, studies, works, and maintains his marriage, but beneath that function there is a persistent sense of threat that has followed him from childhood into adulthood. He speaks about wanting a life that is calm, predictable, and safe, and yet even in moments of peace he often seems to be waiting for the next blow.
